Gender Theory and the Mythodynamics of White Supremacy
abstract: In this article I explore how so-called progressive movements and theories remain ensnared within the mythodynamics of white supremacy. Rather than dismantle modernity’s normative conception of the human, contemporary gender theory is preoccupied with expanding its border boundaries. As such, adherents of the gender theories that dominate the North American, neoliberal academy end up advancing the work of the State and capital by legitimating the gendercidal logics of white supremacist patriarchy which plunge subjugated males deeper into the abyss of violence and death.

title: Critical Reflections on Husserl’s Treatment of the Thing in Itself
abstract: It is a familiar story that, where Kant humbly draws a line beyond which cognition can’t reach, Husserl presses forward to show how we can cognize beyond that limit. Kant supposes that cognition is bound to sensibility and that what we experience in sensibility is mere appearance that does not inform us about the intrinsic nature of things in themselves. By contrast, for Husserl, it makes no sense to say we experience anything other than things in themselves when we enjoy sensory perception. Kant’s conception, then, by doing just that, is nonsensical. I argue that Husserl’s account does not deliver on its promise. Things as they are in themselves are just as cognitively out of reach on Husserl’s understanding of them as they are on Kant’s. Further, the charge of nonsense Husserl raises against Kant’s conception of things in themselves applies—indeed, with greater force—to his own.

title: Capitalism in Frame: A Reconstruction and Critique of Fraser’s Approach to Global Justice
abstract: For more than two decades, Nancy Fraser has produced a unique approach to global justice that is radically critical of capitalism. This paper reconstructs and evaluates that approach by tackling over two dozen of Fraser’s relevant publications and the secondary literature on the topic. My thesis is that Fraser’s approach consists of two complementary parts that can be coherently integrated. The first part operates in the domain of justice, and its main component is Fraser’s post-Westphalian theory of democratic justice. The second part operates in the domain of capitalism, and its main component is Fraser’s neo-Polanyian conception of capitalism. I evaluate the approach against three challenges, which concern (1) theorizing race as a system of domination; (2) decentering the individual and their freedom as the locus of normativity; and (3) accommodating non-Western political and cultural identities and priorities. Fraser’s approach can largely, though not completely, respond to the challenges.

title: Games as Abstract Artifacts
abstract: Recent debates in the ontology of games have primarily focused on questions of individuation and persistence. By contrast, the problem of the nature of games has received limited attention. This paper aims to address this gap by examining what kind of entities games are. After surveying several possible answers to that question, which I argue to be unsuccessful, I explore the view that games are abstract artifacts. I consider how this theory can be developed and motivated, as well as some challenges it faces.

Perfect Trouble: Atomism, Non-Atomism, and the Dilemma of Perfect Being Theology
abstract: Perfect being theology holds that God is the greatest possible being and that the divine nature is fixed by the perfections a being instantiates. In this paper I examine four ways of relating perfections to overall greatness: Distributivist Atomism, Collectivist Atomism, Distributivist Non-Atomism, and Collectivist Non-Atomism. I argue that each approach faces structural difficulties. The atomist views require that all perfections be jointly instantiated at their intrinsic maxima, which raises a substantive worry about whether the relevant set of perfections is compossible at all. The non-atomist and collectivist views avoid that worry by permitting tradeoffs or relation-dependent maxima, but they generate new problems: they fail to single out a unique best package of perfections, they leave unresolved why any one package should fix the divine nature, and—given the standard claim that the greatest possible being exists necessarily—they produce a dilemma involving polytheism or the absence of any greatest possible being.

title: Is Divine Concurrence Possible?
abstract: The doctrine of divine concurrence maintains that, whenever a creaturely or “secondary” cause brings about an effect, the whole of that effect is also directly brought about by God, the “primary” cause. Simon Kittle and Timothy D. Miller have recently (and separately) argued that divine concurrence is incoherent or impossible. This paper responds to the arguments of Kittle and Miller. It also offers two independent reasons, apart from any reasons for thinking the doctrine true, for holding that concurrence is possible.
